terms.definition: The primary accepts writes; replicas copy from it and can take over if it fails.
A periodic probe that decides whether a component is actually serving.
Having spare copies or servers so that one failure need not take the system down.

before.note: Read Replication, Consensus and Circuit Breakers first: failover switches to the replicas that replication provides, it picks exactly one new primary the way consensus elects a leader, and it decides what counts as failed using the kind of health checking circuit breakers rely on. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Failover is the mechanism that turns spare capacity into real availability. Replication gives you standby copies, but a standby does nothing until something notices the primary has failed and switches to it. Amazon frames this concretely for databases: an RDS Multi-AZ deployment keeps one or more standby instances that provide failover support, so when the primary fails a standby can take over [[aws-rds-multiaz]].

The same idea applies to stateless traffic. Cloudflare's load balancer decides which endpoints can handle traffic through a system of monitors, health monitors, and pools: a monitor issues health requests at regular intervals to evaluate each endpoint in a pool, and unhealthy endpoints are dropped [[cf-lb-health]]. Whether it is a database promoting a replica or an edge dropping a sick origin, failover is the loop of detect, decide, redirect.

The reason this is hard, and worth a topic, is that each step can go wrong: detection can mistake a slow node for a dead one, the decision can accidentally pick two replacements, and redirection can stall waiting for caches. Getting all three right and fast is what separates a few seconds of blip from a long outage.

terms.definition: Detecting a failed component and switching to a healthy stand-in so service continues.
A replica kept ready to take over as primary when the current primary fails.
A group of interchangeable endpoints or origins that a load balancer can route among.
The three steps of failover: notice the failure, choose a replacement, send traffic to it.

stages.name: How it works
body: Detection comes first, and the naive version is dangerous. Orchestrator, the MySQL failover tool, warns that a naive monitor just probes the primary and alerts when it cannot reach it, which produces false positives when the primary is merely overloaded. Instead Orchestrator uses a holistic approach: it observes not only the server but also its replicas, and treats the primary as failed only when it cannot reach the primary and the replicas confirm they cannot see it either [[orchestrator-detection]].

Deciding on a replacement must yield exactly one winner. For a single-writer database this is a promotion, and it is backed by agreement so two replicas never both become primary. The old primary must then be fenced, prevented from accepting writes if it returns, or you get split-brain: two primaries taking conflicting writes. Cloudflare's edge case is gentler, because origins are interchangeable and stateless, so steering a request to another healthy origin carries no split-brain risk; the decision there is a health-and-threshold judgement over a pool [[cf-lb-health]].

Redirection has to be fast. If clients find the primary through DNS, they may keep using the old address until the cached record's time-to-live expires. The common fix is to redirect at a layer you control: a managed database updates its endpoint so clients reconnect to the new primary [[aws-rds-multiaz]], and an edge load balancer simply stops sending traffic to the dropped endpoint [[cf-lb-health]], neither waiting on a DNS cache.

terms.definition: Declaring failure only when the server and its replicas agree it is unreachable, cutting false positives.
Turning a chosen replica into the new primary.
Stopping a failed or returned primary from accepting writes, so there is never a second primary.
Two nodes both acting as primary and taking conflicting writes; failover must prevent it.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The deepest tension in detection is slow versus dead. Orchestrator notes that false positives can happen when the primary is overloaded rather than failed, so acting on a single probe risks failing over a database that is actually alive, an self-inflicted outage. Corroborating across the replicas reduces false positives and, Orchestrator notes, also improves response time for real failures because agreement is strong evidence [[orchestrator-detection]]. This is why failover and consensus are relatives: both decide only when a quorum agrees.

For stateful systems, the decision is a point of no return, so it must be exactly one promotion plus fencing. For stateless systems you can be more relaxed and quantitative: Cloudflare evaluates health per pool and even per region, and only when the majority of a region's data centers pass is the region considered healthy, so a few bad probes do not flip routing [[cf-lb-health]]. The threshold is a tuning knob: too twitchy steers on a transient dip, too lax leaves users on a failing endpoint.

There is also a data-loss dimension unique to databases. With synchronous standbys, a failover loses no acknowledged writes; AWS RDS Multi-AZ keeps the standby synchronously updated for exactly this reason [[aws-rds-multiaz]]. With asynchronous replication, a promoted replica may be slightly behind, so you promote the most up-to-date one and accept a small, bounded loss. Stateless failover has no equivalent, which is why edge failover can be faster and simpler than database failover.

terms.definition: Declaring a healthy-but-slow component failed, triggering a needless and harmful failover.
A standby kept exactly in step with the primary, so a failover loses no acknowledged writes.
How many unhealthy members of a pool trigger steering away; a tuning knob against flapping.
Acting only when a majority of observers concur, shared between failover detection and consensus.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: In practice, match the failover design to the tier. For a database, lean on a managed or consensus-backed promotion that guarantees one primary and fences the old one; AWS RDS Multi-AZ does this for you, keeping a synchronous standby and failing over automatically [[aws-rds-multiaz]]. For stateless traffic, health-check origins into pools with a failure threshold and let the edge route around unhealthy ones; Cloudflare decides per data center so a local failure is contained locally [[cf-lb-health]].

Mind the knobs that cause self-inflicted outages. Detection that is too eager flaps; Orchestrator's holistic approach exists precisely to avoid failing over an overloaded-but-alive primary [[orchestrator-detection]]. Redirection that trusts DNS is slow; prefer a layer you control. And after a failover, restore redundancy by attaching a fresh standby, or the next failure has nothing to fail over to.

The unifying lesson is that recovery time is set by the slowest of the three steps, and it is usually redirection, not detection, that dominates when teams rely on DNS. Both tiers converge on the same move: terminate at something you control, a managed endpoint or an edge, so you can switch targets in seconds. Keep failovers rare with good detection, make them safe with one-winner promotion and fencing, and make them fast by owning the redirect.

misconceptions.myth: If I have replicas, I already have high availability.
misconceptions.truth: Replicas are only standbys; without failover to detect failure and switch to them, nothing takes over [[aws-rds-multiaz]].

misconceptions.myth: Fail over the moment a monitor cannot reach the primary.
misconceptions.truth: That causes false positives when the primary is just overloaded; corroborate across its replicas first [[orchestrator-detection]].

misconceptions.myth: Lowering the DNS TTL is a good way to fail traffic over quickly.
misconceptions.truth: Clients may ignore or cache short TTLs; failing over at an edge or endpoint you control is faster and reliable [[cf-lb-health]].

misconceptions.myth: Any replica can be promoted on failure with no data concern.
misconceptions.truth: With asynchronous replication a lagging replica loses writes; a synchronous standby avoids that, which is why RDS keeps one [[aws-rds-multiaz]].
